title: Bodhidharma's Outline of Practice
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Bodhidharma's Outline of Practice in Red Pine's translation, and tells the story of Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu, who hears "No merit" and "I don't know." Joden follows the text's four practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing, and practicing the Dharma. Each gets a short commentary, drawing on Ryokan's lines about meeting disaster, illness, and death, and on a Shodo Harada prayer that begins "I vow to choose what is." Joden offers a New England proverb for wanting less, "Use it up, wear it out, make it do, do without," and closes with Dogen's threefold mind from Instructions to the Tenzo.

Good.
OK.

This is actually a good opening for what I'm going to speak to today, which is Bodhidharma's outline of practice.
Excuse me.
This is based on Red Pine's translation of Zen teachings of Bodhidharma, published in 1987.
It's also found in his anthology called Zen Roots that just came out this year, which I highly recommend.
In our morning service, as we just spoke, we invoke our ancestors who have transmitted the lamp through space and time.
Shakyamuni Buddha in India, Bodhidharma in China, Dogen in Japan, and Shogaku Shunryo Suzuki bringing the Dharma to the West.
We've had many teishos over the years on Buddha, Dogen, and Suzuki Roshi, with Tim's this year focusing on Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
Yesterday, at the Saturday service, we recited the Fukanzazengi of Dogen, where he tells us:
*The way is basically perfect and all-pervading.* *[unclear: "I mentioned"] the Buddha who was possessed of inborn knowledge.
The influence of his six years of upright sitting is noticeable still.
Or Bodhidharma's transmission of the mind seal, the fame of his nine years of wall sitting, three more years than Buddha, is celebrated to this day.*
What I reflected on is that Bodhidharma seems to be the silent leg of the chair we all sit on.
We rarely pay attention to his teachings.
I personally have this, I guess it comes from some of my previous lives, but this personal interest in first causes and root beginnings.
I like to go back to the source of things.
I'd always rather go back to the original than to the successors or the commentaries.
I had a teacher years ago in Buffalo, New York who had a line that says, the first is always the most advanced, in the sense that when something is new, it has broken through the previous barriers.
I think of Bodhidharma that way, coming to China.
I have a friend who focuses his Dharma practice on studying the Heart Sutra.
When he started looking at Bodhidharma's writings, he said, "It's all there."

So today I'd like to bring forward this short text of our foundational guiding teacher who brought the Dharma of Chan Zen form to China, the teacher Roshi Robert Aitken calls the archetype for steadfast practice.
It was striking when I went to Japan with the Mountain Rain Sangha how often we saw statues and images, not so much of Buddha, except in the temples, but of Jizo and Bodhidharma, or Daruma.
You'll see him like this, little dolls.
In Japan, a Daruma doll is a traditional good luck charm for making a wish or setting a goal.
One eye is painted with a circular dot, which I did this morning.
One works towards the goal every day.
Once the goal or wish becomes reality, the other eye is painted on.
So when I finish this talk, hopefully it will allow me to put the other eye on my Daruma.
For the everyday Japanese person, the true meaning of Daruma is as a reminder of self-perseverance, focus and discipline.
A popular idiom, a core Zen proverb that we often refer to and that's often tied to the meaning of Daruma, is Nanakorobi Yaoki, translated roughly as "fall down seven times, stand up eight."
Daruma is a symbol of perseverance and staying the path.
In preparing for this talk today, I've looked to Red Pine's commentaries and those of Shodo Harada Roshi in his text, The Path to Bodhidharma.

Most of you on the screen actually are deep practitioners of Zen, but I thought a little background of our 29th ancestor, as told in Keizan's Transmission of the Light, would be helpful to remind us of Bodhidharma.
He was born in about 440 AD, the third son of King Simhavaran, a Buddhist who invited Prajnatara, the 28th ancestor, from the Buddhist heartland of Magadha, where Buddha himself was enlightened.
He brought him to his court to teach, where he taught Bodhidharma as a young man.
Prajnatara transmitted the Mahayana teachings to Bodhidharma and told him, you should go to China and spread the teachings that point to the mind and nothing else.
In 472, Bodhidharma sailed the coastal route.
If you look at a map, it's a long ways from India all around Malaysia to China, because the overland route was blocked by invaders.
He arrived in China three years later.
The ground for Bodhidharma's arrival in China was prepared by numerous Indian followers of the Buddha carrying the Prajnaparamita texts, beginning about AD 65.
But it wasn't until Bodhidharma arrived that a dedicated practitioner, as opposed to a scholar of meditation, arrived.
Even at that time, there were an estimated 8,500 temples in China and 120,000 clergy of Buddhism.
Less than 50 years later, there were 30,000 temples and over 2 million clergy, over 5% of the population.
Buddhism was spreading rapidly amongst the common people.

There's a pivotal story of Bodhidharma's arrival at the court of King Wu, one of China's great supporters of Buddhism, told in the first koan of the Blue Cliff Record and the second koan in the Book of Serenity.
When he arrived at the court of King Wu, the emperor asked if his bountiful philanthropy hadn't earned him incalculable amounts of merit.
Bodhidharma responded, "No merit."
As Red Pine says, worldly blessing, perhaps, but not merit.
Material philanthropy has no effect on spiritual welfare.
King Wu then asked him, "What is the ultimate meaning of the holy truth?"
Bodhidharma said, "Vast and void, no holiness."
The emperor said, "Who are you facing me?"
Bodhidharma said, "I don't know."
The emperor did not understand the teachings of emptiness, so Bodhidharma left abruptly and went north.
When he crossed the Yangtze River, it is told, he did so on a single hollow reed.
He came to the Shaolin temple, where he sat for nine years, as we just spoke in our opening prayer, and he was known there as the Indian who stares at the wall.
Legend says he cut off his eyelids to stay fully alert, hence his bulging eyes.
And where they fell, tea plants grew to help others stay awake in their meditation practice.
Thank you, Bodhidharma.
Later, Emperor Wu asked his trusted advisors, "Why did that guy leave so quickly, so suddenly?"
His advisor said, "Does your majesty know who that man is?"
The emperor said, "I don't know."
The advisor said, "He is the Mahasatva Avalokiteshvara, transmitting the seal of the Buddha's mind."
The emperor regretted what had happened and wanted to send an emissary to invite Bodhidharma back.
The advisor said, "Your majesty, don't try to send an emissary to fetch him back.
Even if all the people in the land were to go after him, he would not return."
Sometime during this period, after 534, the outline of practice, which I'll speak to in a minute, was written down by a disciple, Tan Lin.
Why is Bodhidharma the most famous of all the millions of monks who studied and taught the Dharma in China?
Zen as meditation had been taught and practiced for several hundred years.
Much of what he had to say concerning doctrine had been said before.
But Bodhidharma's approach to Zen was unique, as he said in the sermons in Red Pine's book: seeing your nature is Zen.
Not thinking about anything is Zen.
Everything you do is Zen.
While others viewed Zen as purification of the mind or a stage on the way to Buddhahood, Bodhidharma equated Zen with Buddhahood and Buddhahood with the mind, the everyday mind.
And here we are today in Bellingham, Washington, or other scattered places, but connected by this Zoom miracle, practicing under the banner of Zoketsu Norman Fishers, every day Zen.
Walls sitting each morning, thanks to Bodhidharma's devotion to practice.
So what does this outline of practice, or more properly, contemplation of four practices for entering the Mahayana path, provide us as encouragement and direction?
First, the bumper sticker version, one I carry around in my head and have for years to remind me of my responsibilities and opportunity to polish the moment.
The four principles of the outline of practice are quite simple.
One, suffer injustice or requite your animosity.
Two, adapt to conditions.
Three, want nothing.
Four, practice Dharma.
We can view these four statements as a kind of rephrasing of the Four Noble Truths.
In the realm of samsara, of suffering, dukkha, as Shuddho Chris has spoken to a number of times, it's an innate characteristic of our existence.
Nothing is permanent: endure suffering.
The origin of suffering is craving or attachment: accept conditions.
Cessation of suffering can be attained by letting go of attachment: want nothing.
The Noble Eightfold Path is the path to renouncement of craving and cessation of suffering: practice Dharma.
Or as Red Pine sums it up, bad karma, good karma, no new karma, Buddha karma.
I like that.
That's the short version, and this whole text is only three pages long in its entirety.
So how does Bodhidharma present these principles?
I'll give you some excerpts.
*Many roads lead to the path, but basically there are only two, reason and practice.*
*To enter by reason means to realize the essence through instruction and to believe that all living things share the same nature.
Those who meditate on walls and the absence of self and others are in complete and unspoken agreement with reason.
Without moving, without effort, they enter, we say, by reason.*
But in our Mahayana tradition, we must bring this embodied understanding to bear in the world of samsara.
We must engage the relative world with our whole hearts, bodies and minds.
Hence the need to bring those understandings to bear through practice.
He goes on to say:
*To enter by practice refers to four inclusive practices: suffering injustice, adapting to conditions, seeking nothing and practicing the Dharma.*
So let's listen to what Bodhidharma says about each of these practices, and I'll make a short commentary on each.

*When those who search for the path encounter adversity, they should think to themselves, "In countless ages gone by, I've turned from the essential to the trivial and wandered through all manner of existence, often angry without cause and guilty of numerous transgressions.
Now, though I do no wrong, I'm punished for my past.
Neither gods nor men can foresee when an evil deed will bear its fruit.
I accept it with an open heart and without complaint of injustice."*
He then quotes from the Vimalakirti Sutra: *When you meet with adversity, don't be upset because it makes sense.* And he goes on to say, *With such understandings, you're in harmony with reason.
And by suffering injustice, you enter the path.* The first principle: just understanding and accepting the basic nature of karma that is our life.
One moment and a continuous line in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
They have all come to this, or as Dongshan tells us, "Just this is it."
This moment now includes the entire universe, everything that has gone before, all to this one moment right now.
By fully accepting and entering this moment, we can take the next step off the 100-foot pole, knowing nothing but confident that all will be provided.
The 19th century Soto Zen monk Ryokan put it this way:
*To meet disaster at the time of disaster is fine, just as it is.
To meet illness in the time of illness is fine, just as it is.
To meet death at the time of death is fine, just as it is.*
Next to my desk hangs a prayer invocation by Shodo Harada Roshi.
I can't remember where I found it, but it begins:
*In this passing moment, karma ripens and all things come to be.
I vow to choose what is.*
And a few lines on:
*If there is a cost, I choose to pay.
If there is sorrow, I choose to weep.
When starving, I choose hunger.
When happy, I choose joy.
When it is my death, I choose to die where this takes me.
I choose to go being with what is.
I respond to what is.*
This is fully embracing the moment, accepting it for the karmic truth that it has.
Indeed, it has all come to this.
Recognizing that this right moment is everything, the second practice is to accept, to adapt to these circumstances.
Bodhidharma here tells us:
*As mortals, we are ruled by conditions, not by ourselves.
All the suffering and joy we experience depends on conditions.
If we should be blessed by some great reward, such as fame or fortune, it is the fruit of seed planted by us in the past.
When conditions change, it ends.
Why delight in its existence?
But while success and failure depend on conditions, the mind neither waxes nor wanes.
Those who remain unmoved by the wind of joy silently follow the path.*
No matter what happens, our practice teaches us to accept without judgment and to respond accordingly.
This is what Hirata Roshi calls being obedient to karma.
When we accept things as they are, we are free to take the next step, without preconception, responding to conditions as they arise.
This is something that our sitting practice teaches us.
Things arise, things pass, arising out of emptiness, passing into emptiness.
No trace left behind.
In our lives, good things apparently happen, bad things apparently happen.
Nothing stays forever.
Fame is fleeting, fortunes too.
Unless we cling to our gains, and then we are caught by them: we then serve our gains rather than our gains serving us and others.
What is there to hold on to?
Our meditation practice offers us the opportunity to simply watch as things come and go.
It puts us in touch with our Buddha nature.
We translate that experience into our day-to-day lives and recognize that within changing circumstances, there is a stable platform.
A platform of emptiness, a place of potential, as Zoketsu has called it, on which our lives rest.
How hard it is sometimes to recall and remember that stability.
The poet Robert Duncan was fond of reconstituting "remember" as "re-member," bringing back into a whole the members or pieces of the situation or circumstances of our lives.
Continuing practice helps us to touch that sense, that feeling of wholeness and sufficiency that is always present, a steadiness in contrast to our passing delusions and misapprehensions.
When we fully meet conditions, no matter how dire or wonderful, with our entire energy and agency, we embody Bodhidharma.
Bodhidharma's third practice is seeking nothing.
He tells us:
*People of this world are deluded.
They are always longing for something, always, in a word, seeking.
But the wise wake up.
They choose reason over custom.
They fix their minds on the sublime and let their bodies change with the seasons.
All phenomena are empty.
They contain nothing worth desiring.
Calamity forever alternates with prosperity.
To dwell in the three realms is to dwell in a burning house.
To have a body is to suffer.
Does anyone with a body know peace?
Those who understand this detach themselves from all that exists and stop imagining or seeking anything.
The sutras say, to seek is to suffer.
To seek nothing is bliss.
When you seek nothing, you're on the path.*

When we chant "all my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate, and delusion," we recognize right up front that craving is fundamental to our unexamined lives, that its roots run deep, and that by stating it as a primary condition, we are aware of its power and fundamental reality.
What then do we do to address this deeply motivating behavior?
How do we find satisfaction and comfort in what is, and not in the endless pursuit of our hungers for material goods, food, or social standing?
Or even enlightenment, however that manifests itself.
The initial recognition of this drive for more, beyond our basic need for food, clothing, and shelter, comes with our sitting practice, watching our cravings coming and going.

A few weeks ago, when discussing the state of our planet during a previous Dharma talk, someone raised the question: how can we address the current dilemma, based on overconsumption of the entire world that we live in, when we are constantly assaulted with ads and social customs that reinforce the urgency of wearing the newest fashion, going to the next best restaurant, or making sure we have the nicest car?
And when we achieve that momentarily desired state, it's very impermanent, and our own fleeting attention brings up the next thing or condition we want.
What or who is doing this wanting?
What happens when we are fully satisfied with what we have in this moment, and then the next and the next?
What do we really need, and how much are our cravings a program we have a choice about whether to respond to or not?
It's an interesting exercise: when you have an instinctive desire to want something, say a brownie or a new piece of clothing, take a moment to ask, why must I gain this thing or condition now?
By asking the question, the answer becomes most obvious.
It is in fact a passing craving.
If it keeps coming up, you may actually be hungry, or need that new car or a piece of clothing because it's broken or worn out.
That's different than wanting, wanting, wanting.
I've always liked the old New England proverb of frugality and simplicity: "Use it up, wear it out, make it do, do without."
Good to remember when we are dissatisfied with our material conditions, when our untrained minds and acquisitive desires are driving us to always want more and more.
Allowing these cravings to come and go, much as we allow our thoughts to come and go without attachment when sitting, is a core part of our living practice.
But it's not only things, it's also our wanting the conditions of our lives to meet certain expectations.

Having these predetermined outcomes in mind, or fearing the various ways they won't be achieved, seems to be at the root of our anxieties, the constant what-if-ing and exhausting preparation for the upcoming moment.
Turn that inside out and reflect: if I want nothing, then what I have is a gift to share, to offer to others.
The first paramita of dana, or generosity, is based on this fundamental stance.
It is the other side of the coin, as they say.
Wanting nothing is also a statement of our faith in the Dharma to constantly provide what we truly need, not what we think or imagine we need.
With this understanding, we have, as Harada Roshi says, never left the Buddha's palm at any time or in any way.
When we give ourselves completely to the Dharma path with our full energy, all is provided.
What we have is fully sufficient in our presence, and the interactions we have with those around us and the infinite world of sentient beings are filled with gladness and joy.
Neither wanting nor holding on to what we have opens the Dharma gate to true joy, embracing and delighting the old but never tired line, "you can't take it with you."
It frees us in this life from the suffering of this saha world.
This brings us to the fourth part of entering through practice, practice in accord with the Dharma.
Here's what the clear, big-eyed Bodhidharma tells us:
*The Dharma is the truth that all natures are pure.
By this truth, all appearances are empty.
Defilement and attachment, subject and object, don't exist.
The sutras say, the Dharma includes no being because it's free from the impurity of being, and the Dharma includes no self because it's free from the impurity of self.
Those wise enough to believe and understand this truth are bound to practice according to the Dharma.

And since that which is real includes nothing worth begrudging, they give their body, life and property in charity without regret, without the vanity of giver, gift or receiver, and without bias or attachment.
And to eliminate impurity, they teach others, but without becoming attached to form.
Thus, through their own practice, they are able to help others and glorify the way of enlightenment.
And as with charity, they also practice the other virtues.
While practicing the six virtues to illuminate delusion, they practice nothing at all.
This is what is meant by practicing the Dharma.*
In our world of craving and competition, we say, "practice makes perfect."
In the Dharma realm, we understand that practice makes practice.
That, as Shunryu Suzuki says, you are perfect the way you are, but there is always room for improvement.
There is no end, thankfully, to this practice, this effortless effort we commit to, sitting on the cushion and living our everyday lives.
This fourth practice is really a statement for living a life based on our experience of great mind, of Buddha Dharma, informing our every action, our every word, our every feeling.
I've always found Dogen's articulation of this all-embracing mind, in his Instructions to the Tenzo, most clarifying.

He instructs us to bring forth our Dharma understanding in our every action of body, speech, and mind as a threefold manifestation: the caring and compassionate parent or grandparent mind, the joyful mind fully embracing each moment of this life, and the magnanimous mind, overwhelmingly generous and constantly offering to others.

Practicing and embodying the six paramitas (generosity, Dharma practice, patience, vigor, concentration, and wisdom) without self-consciousness, fully aware, perhaps only in retrospect but certainly not in the moment, is our fundamental obligation and responsibility as Bodhisattvas on the path.
My hope is that this introduction to a short but profound teaching by our founding teacher will inspire you to investigate thoroughly, as Master Dogen would say, this matter.
My deep gratitude for this opportunity to open this text for you this morning.
Thank you.
I'm drawing a blank.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of the Buddha's way.*
*All beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
The Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
